title: Effects of Video-Based Informed Consent on Patient Acceptance, Knowledge Gain, and Consultation Duration Prior to Radical Prostatectomy or Ureterorenoscopy - A Randomized Mixed-Methods Study
summary:
Background
Before any operation, a doctor must explain to the patient why the operation is needed, how it is done, what risks it carries and what other treatments are available. Only then can the patient make an informed decision and agree to the operation. At present, this explanation usually takes place in a face-to-face conversation, supported by a written information form. However, many people afterwards remember only part of the information or have not understood everything. In other areas of medicine, short explanatory videos have helped: patients knew more afterwards and were more satisfied. For two common operations on the urinary tract, this has not yet been studied. The first is the removal of the prostate in men with prostate cancer. The second is the removal of kidney stones or stones in the tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder, using a thin instrument passed through the urethra.

Research question
We want to find out whether an explanatory video, shown in addition to the usual conversation with the doctor,
- helps patients better understand and remember the most important information about their operation,
- increases satisfaction with the information they receive,
- can shorten the personal conversation with the doctor without lowering patient satisfaction.

We also want to find out:
- how well the video is received by patients and by doctors,
- how doctors experience their workload,
- whether the video changes patients’ fears and worries before the operation.

Methods
300 adults who are scheduled for one of the two operations at Ulm University Hospital will take part, 150 for each operation. Chance decides who will also watch the video. Half of the participants will watch an explanatory video on a tablet before their conversation with the doctor. The other half will receive the usual information without the video, and they can still watch the video once the survey has been completed. Every participant will receive the full personal conversation with the doctor and the written information form. The video adds to the conversation and does not replace it.

Directly after the conversation, and still before the operation, all participants will fill in a paper questionnaire. It contains about 10 questions on what they know about the operation, as well as questions about their satisfaction, how easy the information was to understand and any worries they have about the operation. The length of the conversation with the doctor will be timed with a stopwatch. The 8 doctors who give the information will also fill in questionnaires.

In addition, we will hold individual interviews of 20 to 30 minutes with about 10 patients from the video group and about 5 doctors. These interviews will help us better understand their experiences, any difficulties and their suggestions for improvement. The interviews will be audio-recorded only if participants give separate consent.

Taking part is voluntary. Participants can stop at any time without any disadvantage, and taking part has no effect on their treatment. The study will last no longer than two years.
conditions: Calculus of kidney with calculus of ureter
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Elective urological surgery: 
   - robot-assisted radical prostatectomy for biopsy-confirmed prostate cancer (with or without nerve sparing, with or without lymphadenectomy)
   - ureterorenoscopy with stone extraction (flexible or semi-rigid, with or without laser)
- Capacity to consent and willingness to provide written informed consent
- Sufficient command of German or English to understand the video and the questionnaires
Exclusion criteria:
- Emergency or acute procedures, for example:
   - infected hydronephrosis
   - urosepsis with septic shock
   - acute kidney injury
   - severe pain requiring immediate surgery
   - bladder bleeding that cannot be controlled conservatively
- Severe cognitive impairment or dementia
- Severe hearing or visual impairment preventing meaningful comprehension of the video
- Previous participation in this study (only the first study episode is included)
